title: Firewalls: who may come in
summary: How a firewall reads its rules, why drop looks like a timeout, and which firewall each system uses.

scheme: macOS    pf, and the application firewall
text: A firewall decides, packet by packet, what may come in or go out.
- On Linux the kernel does the filtering (nftables); tools only write the rules.
- Rocky turns firewalld on. Debian installs nftables but filters nothing: nftables.service is off, and /etc/nftables.conf lets everything in until you write rules (ufw only if installed).
- A sample that opens a port always says on which system.
A chain is read from the top, and the first rule that matches with a verdict decides.
- A packet from 203.0.113.9 to port 443 stops on line 2: line 3 never sees it.
- A rule matches only if every part matches: the sender's network, the port.
- When no rule matches, the chain's policy decides; a chain with no policy accepts.
- An accept ends only its own chain: another table's chain on the same hook (firewalld's, Docker's) still sees the packet. A drop is final.
drop throws the packet away and says nothing; reject answers at once.
- A client that waits and then times out: a firewall that drops, a wrong route, or a machine that's off on another network (on yours, it's No route to host).
- firewalld rejects by default: the client sees No route to host, even though the machine is there.
- Refused can also mean nothing listens on that port: ss -tln on the server tells.
On Rocky, firewalld groups rules in zones; --list-all shows what the active one lets in.
- --add-service=https opens 443; --add-port=8080/tcp opens a port that has no service name.
- Without --permanent, the change is lost at the next reload or reboot; with it, --reload applies it now.
- On Debian, sudo nft list ruleset shows every rule; empty means nothing filters.
